tier_reason: First-party Criterion run against bundled SQLite (rusqlite 0.32). The bench code is public (core/dbx-benchmarks/benches/official_db_comparison.rs) and rustc 1.92.0 with the release profile is stated, but no CPU model is given (only 'Windows 11 Pro, x64, 16 GB'), so it cannot be A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: 10,000 records, both engines in memory: INSERT 25.21 ms vs SQLite 29.4 ms (about 1.17x; the README rounds this to '1.16x faster, 25ms vs 29ms'). Point GET: 2.84 ms vs 33.8 ms (about 11.9x, derived from page data; the page itself says both '11x' and '13x'). Full SCAN: 51 µs vs 340 µs (about 6.7x, derived from page data).
corrections.workload: Criterion.rs 0.5 bench official_db_comparison.rs: 10,000 string key/value pairs ('key_{i}' / 'value_data_{i}'). INSERT builds a fresh in-memory DB each iteration; GET does 10,000 point lookups; SCAN reads the whole table. DBX (v0.2.0-beta 'Fast-Path', Database::open_in_memory) vs SQLite (rusqlite 0.32 bundled, Connection::open_in_memory, one BLOB-keyed table). Sled 0.34 and Redb 2.1 run on temp dirs in the same suite.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: rustc 1.92.0 / Cargo 1.92.0, Cargo release profile, Criterion.rs 0.5; SQLite is rusqlite 0.32 with the bundled feature. No extra flags stated.
corrections.hardware: Windows 11 Pro (build 26200) x64 PC, about 16 GB RAM; CPU model not stated.
corrections.caveats: Very small, very new project (4 stars, created Feb 2026, single first-party report dated 3 Apr 2026). No CPU model, and the sample is only 10,000 records. The benchmarks page contradicts itself: INSERT is called both 14% and 18% faster, GET both 11x and 13x, and the conclusion cites older v0.0.6 numbers (INSERT 44.92 ms, SCAN 1.60 ms). The 'Fast-Path' section says DBX scan fell from 340 µs to 51 µs, and 340 µs is also the figure given for SQLite. The bench code does not match the documented method. The doc says SQLite runs inside a transaction, but the code inserts in autocommit mode. SQLite lookups use conn.query_row, which re-prepares the SQL for every one of the 10,000 lookups; that handicaps the 'GET 11-13x' result. The README says Tier 1 is a BTreeMap, but the benchmarks page says DashMap + SkipMap. The README is marketing-heavy and has an unfilled Ko-fi placeholder link. GitHub reports NOASSERTION because the LICENSE file adds a donation/sponsorship section after the standard MIT text; the grant itself is plain MIT. Low confidence.

notes: The README figures (1.16x, 25ms vs 29ms) are on the README and match the fuller table in docs/english/benchmarks.md, so benchmark_url now points to that page, which also has the methodology. The GET and SCAN wins over SQLite are larger, but they rest on a SQLite harness that re-prepares statements. Metadata checked: 4 stars, not a fork or archived, last default-branch (main) commit 2026-04-13 (active), MIT.

tier_reason: First-party 2014 Couchbase numbers against SQLite 3.7.11 (WAL mode) on a Nexus 5, with the hardware and configs stated. No compiler or flags are stated, and the results are read off charts plus 'up to' prose, so it is C. The IEEE TC 2016 ForestDB paper is peer-reviewed, but I could not open it to check for a SQLite comparison (paywalled; the computer.org preprint link returns HTML).

corrections.stars_or_usage: 1,333 stars. The README says production Couchbase Server builds use the 'cb-master' branch (Couchbase Server 6.5 onward), and 'master' is left unsupported for community users. ForestDB was also a Couchbase Lite storage option.
corrections.caveats: The analysis section is inside an HTML comment on the live wiki page. The rendered page shows only 'The new benchmark results and analysis will be available soon' (last edited 2016-01-29), so the numbers come from the page's raw Markdown source. The results date from 2014 and are first-party (Couchbase's own team). The figures are 'up to' values read from charts. Writes are slower than SQLite at batch size 1 because append-only storage causes more write amplification. The README says the default 'master' branch is unsupported and was last committed 2019-05-10. Production fixes went to 'cb-master' (last commit 2024-04-11) and the 'neo' release branch (last commit 2025-11-21).

notes: All three figures (reads up to 8x, writes up to 2.3x at larger batch sizes, mixed up to 7x vs SQLite) appear verbatim in the commented-out raw wiki Markdown, along with the hardware and SQLite config. The record's last_commit 2020-09-02 did not match any branch; the default-branch head is 2019-05-10, so 'abandoned' stands, though Couchbase still patches release branches (neo, 2025-11-21). License Apache-2.0 confirmed; not a fork, not archived.

tier_reason: arXiv preprint (Apr 2020) with first-party results against LevelDB 1.22 and RocksDB 6.4.6. The hardware and software are stated, but there is no public code (the footnote points to github.com/anonymous) and no host compiler or flags. I found no peer-reviewed version via crossref, so it stays C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: About 2x the YCSB-A throughput of LevelDB and RocksDB, but only when stress-ng takes 80% of the CPU (20% left). With no CPU contention, RocksDB (4 background threads) has the shortest running time on the 5 GB run; LUDA comes second and LevelDB last. The paper also says LUDA's compaction is '1x faster' than LevelDB's and '2x faster' than RocksDB's. At 1 KB values it processes a similar amount of data as LevelDB in 46% less running time. Without CPU overhead it has the lowest and most stable 99th-percentile latency. The abstract's 'up to 2x higher throughput and 2x data processing speed' is the best case under CPU contention.
corrections.workload: YCSB-A (0.5/0.5 update-read), 16 B keys, values 128 B-1 KB, 4 MB memtable/SST, 4 KB data blocks. Load 10M pairs (~5 GB), then run another 10M operations, with stress-ng CPU overhead at 0%, 40% and 80%. A separate one-hour latency/robustness run uses 0.1 billion 256 B-value pairs (~50 GB). GPU-accelerated compaction vs stock LevelDB 1.22 and RocksDB 6.4.6.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: CUDA 10.1; host compiler and flags not stated. Prototype built on LevelDB v1.22 (~1K LOC modified, +2.7K LOC CUDA), with Snappy compression not implemented. Compared against RocksDB v6.4.6 with 4 threads; all stores use default parameters and 10-bit Bloom filters.
corrections.caveats: The win depends on CPU contention. The 2x throughput appears only when stress-ng uses 80% of the CPU. With a free CPU, RocksDB finishes the 5 GB run fastest and LUDA is only ahead of LevelDB. LUDA has no Snappy compression, and it compacts about 2x more data than LevelDB at 128 B values. The paper says 'we are ready to open source it', but the footnote only links the anonymized placeholder github.com/anonymous. No public repository was found (GitHub repo search), so has_code=false and repo_url is null. arXiv preprint only; no peer-reviewed version found.

notes: The abstract's 'up to 2x throughput / 2x data processing speed' is quoted accurately. The body shows that the 2x comes only with 80% CPU stress, and RocksDB is fastest when the CPU is free, so the claim was overstated. It is rewritten with its conditions; the tier stays C. The hardware in the record matches Section IV-A exactly.
